subject: sci
title: Energy and Waves: Forms of Energy, Heat Transfer, Waves, and Electricity
objectives: You will identify forms of energy and trace energy conversions, using the law of conservation of energy to explain where “lost” energy goes.
You will calculate kinetic energy (KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>), gravitational potential energy (PE = mgh), and efficiency.
You will distinguish conduction, convection, and radiation and interpret heat-transfer data.
You will describe waves by wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed (v = f × λ) and order the electromagnetic spectrum.
You will apply Ohm’s law (V = IR) to simple series circuits and draw conclusions from circuit data.

slides.title: Energy and Waves: How Energy Moves and Changes
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Name forms of energy and trace energy conversions
  • Use conservation of energy and find “lost” energy
  • Calculate KE = ½mv2 and PE = mgh
  • Tell conduction, convection, and radiation apart
  • Describe waves, use v = f × λ, and order the electromagnetic spectrum
  • Use Ohm’s law, V = IR, on simple circuits

Plan: Warm-up → energy → heat → waves → electricity → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 9 of Science. Last week we studied motion and forces; today we follow the energy. Energy questions show up all over the GED Science test, in physics, but also in ecosystems, weather, and the human body, so this lesson pays off across the whole test. You will learn four formulas today, and the GED usually prints the formula for you, so our job is to know what each letter means, plug in carefully, and read data about energy.
ask: Name one thing you used today that runs on energy. Where did that energy come from? (expected answer: any example, such as a phone running on a battery charged from an outlet; keep it for the first big idea)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Motion and Forces Review
slides.board:
1. A cyclist rides 30 km in 1.5 hours. What is her average speed?
  2. A net force of 12 N pushes a 3.0 kg cart. What is its acceleration? (F = ma)
  3. You push a box with a force of 50 N across 4.0 m of floor. How much work do you do? (W = Fd)
  4. A 1,200 kg car moves at 10 m/s. What is its momentum? (p = mv)
steps: Bridge to today: work is measured in joules, the same unit as energy. Doing work on something gives it energy.

notes.say: These four problems review last week. Give the student about three minutes and have them tell you each answer with its unit before you reveal it. Problem 3 is the bridge into today: when you push the box, you transfer 200 joules of energy to it. Work and energy share the same unit, the joule, because work is energy being moved from one thing to another.
ask: In problem 2, what happens to the acceleration if the cart's mass doubles but the force stays the same? (expected answer: it is cut in half, to 2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
What unit does work come in? (expected answer: joules)
notes.watch: In problem 2, students sometimes multiply 12 × 3.0 = 36. Ask them to rearrange F = ma for a before plugging in: a = F ÷ m.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Forms of Energy
slides.board:
Energy = the ability to do work or cause change. Unit: joule (J).

Kinetic (motion)Potential (stored)
Moving objects (mechanical)Gravitational: height
Thermal: jiggling particlesElastic: stretched or squeezed
Sound: vibrating matterChemical: food, fuel, batteries
Electrical: moving chargesNuclear: center of atoms

Light (radiant energy) is carried by electromagnetic waves.

notes.say: Energy is the ability to make something happen: move, heat up, light up, make noise. Almost every form fits in one of two families. Kinetic energy is energy of motion, and that includes some things you cannot see moving, like the jiggling particles in a hot object or the charges moving in a wire. Potential energy is stored energy, waiting to be released, like a book on a high shelf, a stretched rubber band, or the chemical energy in food and gasoline. Light gets its own row because it is carried by waves, which we cover later today.
ask: Is a battery sitting in a drawer kinetic or potential energy? Which kind? (expected answer: potential; chemical energy)
Is the sound of a drum kinetic or potential? (expected answer: kinetic; the air and drum skin are vibrating)
notes.watch: Students often think thermal energy is potential because it is “stored in” hot things. Remind them heat is the motion of particles, so it is a kind of kinetic energy.

slides.title: Worked Example: Trace the Energy
slides.board:
A hydroelectric dam holds back a lake. Water falls through a pipe, spins a turbine, and a generator sends electricity to homes, where it powers lamps.

Trace the energy from the lake to the lamp.
steps: Start with what is stored: water high behind the dam has gravitational potential energy.
As the water falls, it speeds up: potential becomes kinetic energy of moving water, which spins the turbine.
The generator turns the spinning motion into electrical energy.
In the lamp, electrical energy becomes light and some thermal energy.
Chain: gravitational PE → kinetic → electrical → light + thermal.

notes.say: To trace energy, I always start with where it is stored before anything happens, then follow it one change at a time. Each arrow is one device or event doing a conversion. Notice that the last step makes some thermal energy we did not want; almost every real conversion does that, and that is our next big idea.
ask: Trace a car engine: gasoline to a moving car. (expected answer: chemical → thermal → kinetic, with thermal and sound energy given off)

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Energy Is Conserved
slides.board:
Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves to another object.

Total energy in = useful energy out + “wasted” energy (usually thermal)

“Lost” energy on the GED = energy changed to thermal energy by friction or air resistance.

Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%

notes.say: This is the most important rule of the day. Energy never appears from nothing and never disappears. When a test question says energy was lost, translate it in your head to: energy changed into a form we did not want, almost always thermal energy from friction or air resistance. Efficiency tells you what fraction of the energy went where you wanted it. No real machine is 100 percent efficient, because some energy always ends up as thermal energy.
ask: A motor takes in 500 J and gives 400 J of motion. Where did the other 100 J go? (expected answer: it became thermal energy and maybe sound; it was not destroyed)
What is that motor's efficiency? (expected answer: 400 ÷ 500 = 0.80 = 80%)
notes.watch: Listen for “used up” or “destroyed.” Each time, ask: “What form did it change into?”

slides.title: Worked Example: Where Did the Energy Go?
slides.board:
A roller coaster car starts at rest at the top of a hill with 147,000 J of potential energy. At the bottom, sensors show 132,300 J of kinetic energy.

(a) With no friction, what would its KE be at the bottom?
(b) How much energy changed into other forms?
(c) What percent of the starting energy is that?
steps: (a) With no friction, all the PE becomes KE: 147,000 J.
Where did it go? Friction with the track and air resistance changed it into thermal energy (and some sound).
Check: 132,300 + 14,700 = 147,000 J. The total did not change.

notes.say: The total at the top is our energy budget. At the bottom, everything that is not kinetic energy must have gone somewhere else, so I subtract. Then I name where it went, because GED questions love to ask for the explanation, not just the number. The last line is my favorite check: add the pieces back up and you get the starting total, which is conservation of energy in action.
ask: What would make the car's KE at the bottom closer to 147,000 J? (expected answer: less friction, such as smoother wheels or track)

slides.title: We Do: Conversions and Conservation
slides.board:
1. Trace the energy: a person eats breakfast, then rides a bicycle up a hill.
  2. An electric kettle takes in 200,000 J of electrical energy. The water absorbs 160,000 J of thermal energy. (a) How much energy went elsewhere? (b) What is the kettle's efficiency?
steps: 1. Chemical energy in food → kinetic energy of the rider and bike → gravitational potential energy as they climb. Some becomes thermal energy: the rider warms up.
2(a). 200,000 − 160,000 = 40,000 J went elsewhere, mostly thermal energy that warmed the kettle body and the air.

notes.say: Let's do these together. For the first one, you tell me where the energy starts, and we will build the chain one arrow at a time. For the kettle, tell me which number is the total going in and which is the useful part before you calculate anything.
ask: Why does the rider get hot and sweaty? (expected answer: the body converts some chemical energy into thermal energy, not just motion)
Which number goes on the bottom of the efficiency fraction? (expected answer: the total energy in, 200,000 J)
notes.answer: 1. Chemical (food) → kinetic → gravitational potential, with thermal energy given off. 2(a) 40,000 J. 2(b) 80%.
notes.watch: For efficiency, students sometimes divide 200,000 by 160,000 and get 125%. Efficiency can never be more than 100%, so the useful energy always goes on top.

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Calculating KE and PE
slides.board:
KE = ½mv2   m = mass (kg), v = speed (m/s)

PE = mgh   m = mass (kg), g = 9.8 m/s2, h = height (m)

Both give energy in joules (J).

KE order: square the speed → multiply by mass → take half.

Double the speed → 4× the KE. Double the mass or height → 2× the energy.

notes.say: Here are the two energy formulas. Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed, and the speed is squared, which is the step people forget. So I always do the square first, on its own line. Potential energy is just three numbers multiplied: mass, 9.8 for gravity on Earth, and height. Because speed is squared, doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy, and that is why a crash at 60 miles per hour is so much worse than one at 30.
ask: If a ball's speed triples, how many times as much KE does it have? (expected answer: 3<sup>2</sup> = 9 times)
If a book is moved to a shelf twice as high, what happens to its PE? (expected answer: it doubles)
notes.watch: Two classic errors: forgetting the ½ (answer is twice too big) and not squaring the speed. Have the student say the formula aloud as “half m v squared.”

slides.title: Worked Example: Kinetic Energy
slides.board:
A 1,200 kg car travels at 15 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

What is its kinetic energy at 30 m/s?
steps: At 30 m/s: 302 = 900; 1,200 × 900 = 1,080,000; half is 540,000 J, which is 4 times as much.

notes.say: Watch the order. I square the speed first, then multiply by the mass, then take half. When the speed doubles from 15 to 30, the kinetic energy does not double; it becomes four times as large. That is the squared speed at work.
ask: What answer would you get if you forgot the ½ at 15 m/s? (expected answer: 270,000 J, double the correct answer)

slides.title: Worked Example: Potential Energy
slides.board:
A 60 kg hiker climbs to a lookout 150 m above the trailhead.

(a) How much gravitational potential energy has she gained?

(b) A 2.0 kg rock sits at the lookout’s edge, 150 m up. How much KE would it have just before landing at the trailhead level, ignoring air resistance?
steps: With no air resistance, all of that PE becomes KE: 2,940 J just before landing.

notes.say: Potential energy is the easy formula: multiply the three numbers. Part (b) shows how conservation connects the two formulas. As the rock falls, it loses height and gains speed, so potential energy turns into kinetic energy. Ignoring air resistance, the KE at the bottom equals the PE at the top.
ask: Where is the rock's energy all potential, and where is it all kinetic? (expected answer: all potential at the top, all kinetic just before it lands)

slides.title: We Do: KE and PE
slides.board:
1. A 7.0 kg bowling ball rolls at 4.0 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
  2. A 2.0 kg textbook sits on a shelf 1.5 m above the floor. Find its gravitational potential energy.
  3. A truck doubles its speed. By what factor does its KE change?
steps: 3. 22 = 4, so the KE becomes 4 times as large.

notes.say: We will do these one at a time. For each one, tell me the formula first, then which number goes with which letter, then the answer with its unit. I want to hear the square step out loud on problem 1.
ask: What is v<sup>2</sup> in problem 1? (expected answer: 16)
Which number in problem 2 is g? (expected answer: 9.8)
notes.watch: On problem 1, the most common wrong answers are 112 J (no ½) and 14 J (½ × 7.0 × 4.0, no square).

slides.title: Your Turn: Energy Calculations
slides.board:
1. A 0.15 kg baseball is thrown at 40 m/s. Find its KE.
  2. A 5.0 kg box sits on a shelf 2.0 m high. Find its PE.
  3. A machine takes in 500 J and does 400 J of useful work. What is its efficiency, and where did the rest go?
steps: 3. 400 ÷ 500 = 80%; the other 100 J became thermal energy (and maybe sound).

notes.say: Work these alone. You have four minutes. Write the formula first for each one, and tell me your answers with units when you are done. I will reveal them only after you commit.
notes.answer: 1. 120 J. 2. 98 J. 3. 80%; the remaining 100 J changed into thermal energy (and possibly sound) through friction. It was not destroyed.
notes.watch: For problem 1, 240 J means the ½ was skipped; 3 J means the speed was not squared (½ × 0.15 × 40).

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Heat Transfer
slides.board:
Heat always flows from warmer → cooler. “Cold” does not flow.

MethodHowExample
ConductionDirect contactPan handle gets hot
ConvectionWarm fluid rises, cool sinks, making a currentHeater warms a room
RadiationElectromagnetic waves; no matter neededSun warms Earth

Conductors (metals) move heat fast. Insulators (foam, wool, plastic, trapped air) slow it.

notes.say: Thermal energy only flows one way on its own: from the warmer thing to the cooler thing. When you hold ice, cold is not flowing into your hand; heat is flowing out of your hand into the ice. There are three ways heat travels. Conduction needs touching. Convection needs a moving liquid or gas. Radiation needs nothing at all, which is how the Sun's energy crosses 93 million miles of empty space. A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot fast because metal is a good conductor; a plastic spoon does not, because plastic is an insulator.
ask: Why does a down jacket keep you warm? (expected answer: the feathers trap air, an insulator, which slows heat flowing out of your body)
How does the Sun's energy reach Earth? (expected answer: radiation; space is nearly empty, so conduction and convection cannot work)
notes.watch: “The ice pack sends cold into my knee” is the classic error. Restate it: heat leaves the warmer knee and flows into the cooler ice pack.

slides.title: Worked Example: Name the Method
slides.board:
For each one, say which way heat flows and how.

  1. You feel the heat of a campfire on your face from 2 meters away.
  2. A pot of water heats from the bottom, and the water starts to churn in circles.
  3. A cold drink can sits on a warm picnic table.
steps: Ask three questions: Touching? Moving fluid? Across a gap with no touching?
1. Fire → face, across a gap, no touching: radiation (infrared waves).
2. Bottom water → top water: warm water rises and cool water sinks, a moving fluid: convection.
3. Table → can (warmer to cooler), direct contact: conduction.

notes.say: I use the same three questions every time. Is there touching? That is conduction. Is a liquid or gas moving and carrying the heat? That is convection. Is energy crossing a gap with nothing touching? That is radiation. Then I name the direction of flow: always from the warmer object to the cooler one.
ask: In problem 3, does the can warm the table or does the table warm the can? (expected answer: the warmer table warms the cooler can)

slides.title: We Do: Read Heat Transfer Data
slides.board:
Four identical mugs start with 80 °C water in a 22 °C room. Water temperature after 30 minutes:

WrappingNoneFoilWoolFoam
Temp. (°C)48566771
  1. Which way did heat flow?
  2. How many degrees did each mug cool?
  3. Which wrapping is the best insulator?
steps: 1. From the warmer water (80 °C) to the cooler room air (22 °C).
3. Foam: it cooled the least, so it slowed heat transfer the most.

notes.say: GED heat questions usually come with data, so let's read a table together. First the direction of flow, then the change for each mug, then the conclusion. The best insulator is the one with the smallest temperature drop, not the biggest number in the table, so we have to subtract first.
ask: What is the control in this experiment? (expected answer: the mug with no wrapping)
What is the independent variable? (expected answer: the type of wrapping)
notes.watch: Some students pick the mug with the lowest temperature, 48 °C, as best. That mug lost the most heat, so it is the worst.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Waves
slides.board:
A wave carries energy from place to place, not matter.

  • Wavelength (λ): crest to crest, in m
  • Frequency (f): waves per second, in hertz (Hz)
  • Amplitude: height from rest; bigger = more energy

Wave speed: v = f × λ   (m/s)

figure.alt: A wave drawn across a dashed rest line. A double arrow from one crest to the next crest is labeled wavelength. A vertical double arrow from the rest line down to a trough is labeled amplitude. The high points are crests and the low points are troughs.

notes.say: A wave is a traveling disturbance. When a wave passes through the ocean, a floating bottle bobs up and down but mostly stays put; the energy moves, the water does not travel along with it. Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. Frequency is how many waves pass each second, measured in hertz. Amplitude is the height from the rest line, and more amplitude means more energy: a louder sound, a brighter light, a bigger ocean wave. The speed formula ties them together: frequency times wavelength.
ask: On the diagram, is the wavelength crest to crest, or crest to trough? (expected answer: crest to crest, one full cycle)
A radio is turned up louder. Which wave property changes? (expected answer: amplitude)
notes.watch: Students often measure wavelength from a crest to the next trough. That is only half a wavelength.

slides.title: Worked Example: Wave Speed
slides.board:
(a) Water waves on a lake have a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 3.0 m. What is their speed?

(b) A radio station broadcasts at 1.0 × 108 Hz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 108 m/s. What is the wavelength?
steps: Unit check: Hz means “per second,” so (1/s) × m = m/s. Speed comes out in m/s.

notes.say: Part (a) is straight substitution. For part (b) we want the wavelength, so I rearrange first: wavelength equals speed divided by frequency. It works just like the triangle method for speed, distance, and time. Then I check units, which catches a lot of mistakes.
ask: If the radio frequency doubled but the speed stayed the same, what would happen to the wavelength? (expected answer: it would be cut in half)

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Two Kinds of Waves
slides.board:
Mechanical waves need matter: sound, water waves, earthquake waves. Sound cannot cross empty space.

Electromagnetic waves travel through empty space at 3.0 × 108 m/s.

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma

→ shorter wavelength, higher frequency, more energy

Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens

notes.say: There are two kinds of waves. Mechanical waves, like sound, need something to travel through, so in space no one can hear you. Electromagnetic waves, which include light, do not need matter, and they all travel at the same speed in space. The electromagnetic spectrum lists them from longest wavelength to shortest. Moving to the right, frequency goes up and the energy of each wave goes up. That is why ultraviolet gives you a sunburn and X-rays need a lead apron, while radio waves pass through you harmlessly.
ask: Which has more energy, infrared or ultraviolet? (expected answer: ultraviolet; it is further right, with shorter wavelength and higher frequency)
Can sound travel from the Moon to Earth? (expected answer: no; sound needs matter, and space is nearly empty)
notes.watch: Students sometimes think radio waves are the strongest because they travel far. Distance traveled is not energy per wave. Go back to the rule: shorter wavelength = higher frequency = more energy.

slides.title: We Do: Waves
slides.board:
1. A wave on a rope has a frequency of 5.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.40 m. Find its speed.
  2. Put in order from lowest to highest frequency: X-rays, radio waves, visible light, microwaves.
  3. Two sound waves travel through the same air at the same speed. Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B. Compare their wavelengths.
steps: 2. Radio, microwaves, visible light, X-rays (the same order as the spectrum, left to right).
3. Same speed, so f × λ is the same for both. Double f means half the wavelength: A’s wavelength is half of B’s.

notes.say: Let's work these together. Problem 1 is the formula. Problem 2 is the memory sentence. Problem 3 is reasoning with the formula: if the product stays the same and one factor doubles, the other must be cut in half.
ask: Say the memory sentence. (expected answer: Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens)
If wave A's wavelength is 0.5 m, what is wave B's? (expected answer: 1.0 m)
notes.answer: 1. 2.0 m/s. 2. Radio, microwaves, visible, X-rays. 3. Wave A has half the wavelength of wave B.
notes.watch: On problem 3, students often say the wave with the higher frequency is faster. In the same material, all sound waves travel at the same speed.

slides.title: Big Idea 7: Circuits and Ohm's Law
slides.board:
A circuit is a closed loop: source + wires + load. An open switch stops the current.

  • Voltage (V), volts: the push
  • Current (I), amperes (A): the flow
  • Resistance (R), ohms (Ω): what slows the flow

V = I × R   I = V ÷ R   R = V ÷ I

Series: one path; Rtotal = R1 + R2; one bulb out, all out. Parallel: separate paths; one out, others stay on.

notes.say: Electricity is energy carried by moving charges, and it needs a complete loop. Think of water in a hose: voltage is the pressure pushing it, current is how much flows per second, and resistance is how narrow the hose is. Ohm's law connects them: voltage equals current times resistance. If the voltage stays the same and the resistance goes up, the current goes down. In a series circuit there is only one path, so the resistances add and one burned-out bulb breaks the whole loop. Homes are wired in parallel, so turning off one lamp does not turn off the refrigerator.
ask: In the series diagram, what is the total resistance? (expected answer: 4 + 2 = 6 Ω)
In the parallel diagram, if branch A breaks, does branch B stay on? (expected answer: yes, it still has its own complete path)
notes.watch: Students often think more resistance means more current. Use the hose: a narrower hose lets less water through.

slides.title: Worked Example: Ohm's Law
slides.board:
(a) A 9.0 V battery is connected to a 3.0 Ω resistor. Find the current.

(b) A lamp on a 120 V outlet draws 0.50 A. Find its resistance.

(c) The 12 V series circuit in the diagram has a 4.0 Ω and a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find the current.

notes.say: For each part, I find which two values I know and which one I want, then I pick the matching form of Ohm's law. Part (c) adds one step: in a series circuit, add the resistances to get the total before you divide.
ask: In part (c), what current would you get if you used only the 4.0 Ω resistor? (expected answer: 3.0 A, which is wrong because both resistors are in the loop)

slides.title: Your Turn: Heat and Waves
slides.board:
1. Name the method: (a) a hair dryer blows hot air that warms a cold room; (b) your hand melts an ice cube you are holding; (c) a heat lamp keeps food warm from above.
  2. An ocean wave has a frequency of 0.20 Hz and a wavelength of 25 m. Find its speed.
  3. Which has a longer wavelength, microwaves or ultraviolet?
steps: 1. (a) Convection (moving warm air). (b) Conduction (touching; heat flows from hand to ice). (c) Radiation (infrared waves across a gap).
3. Microwaves: they are further left in the spectrum (longer wavelength, lower frequency).

notes.say: Three minutes, on your own. For problem 1, use the three questions: touching, moving fluid, or across a gap. Tell me your answers when you are ready.
notes.watch: For 1(a), some students say radiation because the dryer is hot. The heat reaches the room because the air itself moves, which is convection.

slides.title: Your Turn: Circuits
slides.board:
1. A current of 0.25 A flows through a 48 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?
  2. A phone charger supplies 5.0 V and pushes 2.0 A through a device. Find the device’s resistance.
  3. A 6.0 V battery runs a series circuit with a 1.0 Ω and a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find the current.
  4. The voltage stays the same and the resistance goes up. What happens to the current?

notes.say: Your turn on circuits. Four minutes. Before each calculation, say to yourself which form of Ohm's law you need. Then tell me your answers with units.
notes.watch: On problem 3, watch for 6.0 A or 3.0 A from using only one resistor. Both are in the single loop, so add them first.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Kinetic Energy
slides.board:
A 60 kg runner is moving at 5.0 m/s. Kinetic energy can be calculated with KE = ½mv2.

What is the runner’s kinetic energy?

A. 150 J
B. 300 J
C. 750 J
D. 1,500 J
steps: A is out. 150 J is ½ × 60 × 5.0: the speed was never squared.
B is out. 300 J is just 60 × 5.0, mass times speed. That is momentum’s formula, not kinetic energy.
D is out. 1,500 J is 60 × 25: the speed was squared, but the ½ was left out.
C is correct. v2 = 25; 60 × 25 = 1,500; half of 1,500 = 750 J.

notes.say: On the GED, calculation questions are built from mistakes. Each wrong answer here is what you get from one specific slip, so if your answer matches a choice, that does not prove it is right. Watch how I explain where each wrong choice comes from.
ask: Which wrong answer comes from last week's formula? (expected answer: 300 J, which is mass times speed, the momentum formula)
notes.answer: C. 750 J. A skips the square, B is mass × speed, D skips the ½.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Circuit Data
slides.board:
A student keeps the same battery and changes only the resistor.

Resistance (Ω)3.06.09.018
Current (A)3.01.51.00.50

Which conclusion do the data support?

A. Current increases as resistance increases.
B. The battery supplies about 9.0 V in every trial.
C. A 12 Ω resistor would carry about 1.2 A.
D. Current and resistance change by the same amount.
steps: A is out. Read the rows: as resistance goes up, current goes down.
C is out. V = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 V, so a 12 Ω resistor carries 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A, not 1.2 A.
D is out. From 3.0 to 6.0 Ω, resistance rises by 3.0 while current falls by 1.5. They do not change by the same amount, and they move in opposite directions.
B is correct. I × R = 9.0 in every column (3.0 × 3.0, 1.5 × 6.0, 1.0 × 9.0, 0.50 × 18), and V = IR.

notes.say: Data questions on circuits almost always come back to Ohm's law. My move is to multiply current by resistance in each column and see what stays the same. Once I know the voltage, I can test every choice with a quick calculation.
ask: What current would a 36 Ω resistor carry? (expected answer: 9.0 ÷ 36 = 0.25 A)
notes.answer: B. Current × resistance = 9.0 V in every trial. A reverses the trend; C miscalculates (the correct current is 0.75 A); D misdescribes the change.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Formula, Plug In, Check
slides.board:
1. Write the formula on your scratch paper, even if the question gives it.
  2. Plug in each number under its letter, with units.
  3. Calculate one step per line with the calculator (square first in KE).
  4. Check: is your answer exactly double, half, or the square root of another choice? Those are mistake answers.

No formula needed? Ask: Where did the energy go? and Which way does heat flow?

notes.say: This is the routine for every energy, wave, and circuit calculation on the GED. The test usually gives you the formula, so the points are won or lost in the substitution. Writing each number under its letter takes ten seconds and prevents most errors. Then look at the choices: if your answer is exactly double another choice, you may have forgotten the half, and if it is a perfect square of another, you may have skipped a square root. For the non-calculation questions, the two questions at the bottom answer most of them.
ask: You get 1,500 J on a KE question and 750 J is also a choice. What should you check? (expected answer: whether you took half)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Energy is behind everything that happens: a car moving, a phone charging, the Sun warming your skin. On the GED Science test, you will trace how energy changes form, use a few simple formulas, and read data about heat, waves, and electricity. When a question needs a formula, it is usually printed in the question or the passage, so your job is to know what each letter means and plug in carefully. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Name the forms of energy and trace energy conversions.
  • Use the law of conservation of energy and explain “lost” energy.
  • Calculate kinetic energy (KE = ½mv2) and potential energy (PE = mgh).
  • Tell conduction, convection, and radiation apart.
  • Describe waves, use v = f × λ, and order the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Use Ohm’s law, V = IR, on simple circuits and read circuit data.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Keep a calculator and scratch paper nearby.

screens.title: Forms of energy
screens.html:
Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. It is measured in joules (J). Most forms of energy belong to one of two families.

Kinetic energy (motion)Potential energy (stored)
A moving object: a rolling ball, windGravitational: an object held up high
Thermal: the jiggling of particles (heat)Elastic: a stretched spring or rubber band
Sound: vibrating air or other matterChemical: food, fuel, batteries
Electrical: charges moving in a wireNuclear: the center (nucleus) of atoms

Light, or radiant energy, is carried by electromagnetic waves. Treat it as its own form.

A quick test: if something is moving (even tiny particles), it has kinetic energy. If energy is waiting to be released, it is potential energy.

options: A stretched rubber band, ready to be let go
A bowling ball rolling quickly down the lane
The sound coming out of a radio speaker
Warm air blowing out of a heating vent
why: The ball is moving, so its energy is kinetic, not stored. Potential energy is waiting to be released.
Sound is vibrating air, which is motion, so it is a kind of kinetic energy.
Warm air carries thermal energy, the motion of particles, and it is also moving. That is kinetic energy.
check.hint: Look for energy that is stored and waiting, not energy that is already moving.
check.explain: The stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy. When it is let go, that stored energy becomes kinetic energy. The rolling ball, the sound, and the warm air all involve motion (of the ball, of air, of particles), so they are kinds of kinetic energy.

screens.title: Energy conversions
screens.html:
Energy often changes from one form to another. This is called an energy conversion. To trace one, follow three steps:

  1. Find where the energy is stored before anything happens.
  2. Follow it through each device or event, one arrow at a time.
  3. Name what comes out at the end, including any thermal energy given off.

Almost every real conversion gives off some thermal energy that nobody wanted, like the warmth of a phone charger or a light bulb.

example.prompt: Trace the energy in a battery-powered flashlight that is switched on.
steps: When the switch closes, the battery pushes charges through the wires: electrical energy.
The bulb changes electrical energy into light and some thermal energy.

check.prompt: A solar panel on a roof powers a ceiling fan. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions?
options: Light energy → electrical energy → kinetic energy
Electrical energy → light energy → kinetic energy
Chemical energy → light energy → electrical energy
Kinetic energy → electrical energy → light energy
why: This starts in the wrong place. The panel does not begin with electricity; it receives light from the Sun and turns it into electricity.
No chemical energy is involved here: there is no fuel, food, or battery in this chain. The energy starts as sunlight.
This sequence runs backward. It describes something like a hand-cranked flashlight, not a solar panel running a fan.
check.hint: Where does a solar panel's energy come from? What does a fan do with energy?
check.explain: The panel absorbs light energy from the Sun and changes it into electrical energy. The fan's motor changes electrical energy into kinetic energy of the spinning blades (plus a little sound and thermal energy). The reversed chain (kinetic → electrical → light) describes a hand-cranked flashlight instead.

screens.title: Energy is conserved
screens.html:
Law of conservation of energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves to another object. The total stays the same.

When a GED question says energy was “lost,” ask: What did it turn into? Usually, friction or air resistance changed some of it into thermal energy, which spread into the surroundings.

Total energy in = useful energy out + other forms (mostly thermal)

Efficiency tells what share of the energy went where you wanted it:
efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%

example.prompt: A roller coaster car has 147,000 J of potential energy at the top of a hill. At the bottom it has 132,300 J of kinetic energy. How much energy changed into other forms?
steps: Friction with the track and air resistance changed it into thermal energy (and some sound).
Check: 132,300 + 14,700 = 147,000 J. The total is unchanged.
example.answer: 14,700 J became thermal energy and sound. Nothing was destroyed.

check.prompt: An electric motor takes in 800 J of electrical energy. It produces 600 J of useful kinetic energy. How many joules of energy changed into other forms, such as thermal energy and sound?

mistakes.why: You added the two amounts. The 600 J of motion is part of the 800 J that went in, so subtract: 800 − 600 = 200 J.
75 is the efficiency in percent (600 ÷ 800 × 100). The question asks for the joules that went to other forms: 800 − 600 = 200 J.
Energy is not destroyed, but it does change form. 800 J went in and only 600 J came out as motion, so 200 J became other forms.

check.hint: Energy in = useful energy out + energy in other forms.
check.explain:
800 J in = 600 J useful + other forms
800 − 600 = 200 J

That 200 J was not destroyed; friction inside the motor changed it into thermal energy and some sound. (The motor's efficiency is 600 ÷ 800 = 75%.)

screens.title: Calculating kinetic energy
screens.html:
Kinetic energy depends on an object's mass and speed.

KE = ½mv2
m = mass in kilograms (kg), v = speed in meters per second (m/s), KE in joules (J)

Do the steps in this order:

  1. Square the speed (v × v).
  2. Multiply by the mass.
  3. Take half (divide by 2).

The two most common mistakes are forgetting to square the speed and forgetting the ½. Write v2 on its own line every time.

example.prompt: A 50 kg skateboarder rolls at 4.0 m/s. Find her kinetic energy.

check.prompt: A 4.0 kg cart moves at 3.0 m/s. Use KE = ½mv2 to find its kinetic energy in joules.

mistakes.why: 36 is 4.0 × 9.0. You squared the speed and multiplied by the mass but forgot to take half: 36 ÷ 2 = 18 J.
You did not square the speed: ½ × 4.0 × 3.0 = 6. Square first: 3.0<sup>2</sup> = 9.0.
12 is mass × speed (4.0 × 3.0), which is momentum, not kinetic energy. Use ½ × m × v<sup>2</sup>.

check.hint: Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass, then take half.
check.explain:
v2 = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0
4.0 × 9.0 = 36
36 ÷ 2 = 18 J

If you got 36 J, you left out the ½.

screens.title: Calculating potential energy
screens.html:
Gravitational potential energy depends on mass and height. The higher and heavier an object is, the more energy it stores.

PE = mgh
m = mass (kg), g = 9.8 m/s2 (gravity on Earth), h = height (m), PE in joules (J)

Just multiply the three numbers. Do not forget g: the 9.8 is part of every PE calculation on Earth, even when the question only gives you mass and height.

example.prompt: A 3.0 kg flower pot sits on a balcony 8.0 m above the ground. Find its gravitational potential energy.

check.prompt: A 5.0 kg box sits on a shelf 2.0 m above the floor. Use PE = mgh, with g = 9.8 m/s2, to find its gravitational potential energy in joules.

mistakes.why: You multiplied only mass and height (5.0 × 2.0). Include g: 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 98 J.
You took half, but PE = mgh has no ½. That belongs to the kinetic energy formula. 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 98 J.
You added the three numbers (5.0 + 9.8 + 2.0). The formula multiplies them: 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 98 J.

check.explain:
PE = mgh = 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0
5.0 × 9.8 = 49
49 × 2.0 = 98 J

A common error is leaving out g and getting 10.

screens.title: How speed and height change energy
screens.html:
You can answer many GED questions without a full calculation by knowing how the formulas behave.

ChangeEffect on energy
Double the massKE and PE double (×2)
Double the heightPE doubles (×2)
Double the speedKE becomes 22 = 4 times as large
Triple the speedKE becomes 32 = 9 times as large

Speed matters most because it is squared. This is why a car crash at highway speed is far more damaging than one in a parking lot.

example.prompt: A 1,200 kg car has 135,000 J of kinetic energy at 15 m/s. How much does it have at 30 m/s?

check.prompt: A ball's speed triples while its mass stays the same. Its new kinetic energy is how many times its old kinetic energy? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: That would be true if KE grew in step with speed, but speed is squared in KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>. Tripling speed gives 3<sup>2</sup> = 9 times the KE.
You multiplied 3 by 2. Squaring means multiplying the number by itself: 3 × 3 = 9.
You may have squared 3 and then taken half. The ½ is already part of both the old and new KE, so it cancels out. The ratio is 3<sup>2</sup> = 9.

check.hint: In KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>, the speed is squared.
check.explain: KE depends on v2. If v becomes 3v, then v2 becomes (3v)2 = 9v2. The kinetic energy is 9 times as large.

screens.title: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy
screens.html:
Conservation of energy connects the two formulas. When an object falls, it loses height and gains speed: potential energy turns into kinetic energy. When it is thrown upward, kinetic energy turns back into potential energy.

  • At the top (at rest): all PE, no KE.
  • Halfway down: half PE, half KE.
  • Just before landing: all KE (ignoring air resistance).

If there is no friction or air resistance, KE at the bottom = PE at the top. In real life, the KE at the bottom is a little less, because some energy became thermal energy.

example.prompt: A 2.0 kg rock sits on a cliff 150 m high. How much kinetic energy does it have just before it lands, if air resistance is ignored?
steps: With no air resistance, all of the PE becomes KE.

check.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball is held 10 m above the ground and dropped. Ignore air resistance. Using PE = mgh (g = 9.8 m/s2), how much kinetic energy does the ball have just before it hits the ground?
options: 0 J
why: You took half of the PE. The ½ belongs to the KE formula; with no air resistance, all 196 J of PE becomes KE.
PE is zero at ground level, but the energy has not vanished. It has changed into KE, so the ball has 196 J of KE just before impact.
19.6 is mass × g; you left out the height. PE = 2.0 × 9.8 × 10 = 196 J, and all of it becomes KE.
check.hint: Find the PE at the top. With no air resistance, where does all of it go?
check.explain: PE at the top = 2.0 × 9.8 × 10 = 196 J. As the ball falls, PE changes into KE. With no air resistance, nothing is changed into thermal energy, so the KE just before impact is also 196 J. Taking half (98 J) mixes in the KE formula where it does not belong.

screens.title: Heat flow and conduction
screens.html:
Thermal energy (heat) always flows from a warmer object to a cooler one. It never flows from cooler to warmer on its own. “Cold” is not a thing that flows; when something feels cold, heat is leaving you.

Conduction is heat transfer by direct contact. Fast-moving particles in the warm object bump into slower particles in the cool object and pass energy along. A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot all the way up the handle by conduction.

  • Conductors let heat move easily: metals such as copper, aluminum, and iron.
  • Insulators slow heat transfer: foam, wool, plastic, wood, and trapped air.

A winter coat does not add heat. It slows the heat leaving your body.

check.prompt: You hold a can of soda straight from the refrigerator, and your hand starts to feel cold. Which statement best explains why?
options: Thermal energy flows from your warmer hand into the cooler can by conduction.
Cold flows from the can into your hand by conduction through your skin.
Thermal energy flows from the cooler can into your warmer hand by radiation.
Cold air from the can sinks onto your hand and cools it by convection.
why: Cold does not flow. Your hand feels cold because heat is leaving it and moving into the can.
Heat never flows from cooler to warmer on its own, and your hand is touching the can, which is conduction, not radiation.
Your hand is touching the can directly, so the main transfer is conduction, and it is heat leaving your hand, not cold arriving.
check.hint: Which object is warmer? Heat always moves from warmer to cooler.
check.explain: Your hand is warmer than the can, so heat flows out of your hand into the can. Because they are touching, the transfer is conduction. Your hand feels cold because it is losing thermal energy, not because “cold” is entering it.

screens.title: Convection and radiation
screens.html:
Convection is heat transfer by a moving liquid or gas. Warm fluid is less dense, so it rises; cooler fluid sinks to take its place. This loop is a convection current. Examples: a space heater warming a whole room, water churning in a pot, warm ocean currents.

Radiation is heat transfer by electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared. It needs no matter at all, so it works across empty space. Examples: the Sun warming Earth, feeling a campfire from a few feet away, a heat lamp over food.

AskIf yes
Are the objects touching?Conduction
Is a liquid or gas moving and carrying the heat?Convection
Does energy cross a gap with nothing touching?Radiation

check.prompt:
Complete each sentence.

Sunlight warms the seats of a parked car mainly by {{0}}. A floor heater warms the air near it, and that warm air rises and spreads through the room by {{1}}. A pan handle gets hot while the pan sits on a burner by {{2}}.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: The Sun is not touching the seats; there are about 93 million miles of mostly empty space in between. Energy that crosses a gap travels by radiation.
Convection needs moving air or water to carry the heat. Sunlight crosses empty space as electromagnetic waves, which is radiation.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: Conduction needs touching. Here the warm air itself moves around the room, carrying the heat, which is convection.
The heat spreads because the air moves and circulates, not by waves crossing a gap. A moving fluid means convection.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: The handle is a solid; nothing in it flows. Heat passes from particle to particle through the metal, which is conduction.
The heat reaches the handle by traveling through the touching metal of the pan, not across a gap. That is conduction.

check.hint: Touching = conduction. Moving liquid or gas = convection. Across a gap = radiation.
check.explain: Radiation: sunlight reaches the seats as electromagnetic waves across space. Convection: warm air rises and circulates, carrying heat around the room. Conduction: heat moves through the solid metal from the hot pan to the handle.

screens.title: Parts of a wave
screens.html:
A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from place to place without carrying matter along. A floating bottle bobs up and down as ocean waves pass, but it stays in about the same place.

  • Crest: a high point. Trough: a low point.
  • Wavelength (λ, lambda): the distance from one crest to the next crest (one full cycle), in meters.
  • Amplitude: the height from the rest line to a crest (or down to a trough). A larger amplitude means more energy: a louder sound, a brighter light, a taller ocean wave.
  • Frequency (f): the number of waves that pass a point each second, in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.

figure.alt: A wave drawn across a dashed rest line. A double arrow from one crest to the next crest is labeled wavelength. A vertical double arrow from the rest line down to a trough is labeled amplitude. The high points are crests and the low points are troughs.

check.prompt: Use the diagram. What is the wavelength of this wave, in meters?

figure.alt: A wave drawn above a distance scale marked 0 to 8 meters. The crests are at 1 m and 5 m, and the troughs are at 3 m and 7 m. A vertical scale shows the crests reach +0.5 m and the troughs reach -0.5 m from the rest line.

mistakes.why: You measured from a crest (1 m) to the next trough (3 m). That is only half a wave. Wavelength is crest to crest: 5 − 1 = 4 m.
0.5 m is the amplitude, the height of a crest above the rest line. Wavelength is a horizontal distance, crest to crest.
8 m is the whole length of the drawing, which shows two full waves. One wavelength is crest to crest: 5 − 1 = 4 m.

check.hint: Find two crests next to each other and read their positions on the distance scale.
check.explain: The crests are at 1 m and 5 m. Wavelength = 5 − 1 = 4 m. (The troughs at 3 m and 7 m give the same answer.) The 0.5 m on the side scale is the amplitude, not the wavelength.

screens.title: Wave speed: v = f × λ
screens.html:
The speed of a wave equals its frequency times its wavelength.

v = f × λ
v = speed (m/s), f = frequency (Hz), λ = wavelength (m)

Rearranged: λ = v ÷ f   and   f = v ÷ λ

Unit check: Hz means “per second,” so (1/s) × m = m/s, a speed. If your units do not come out as m/s, you divided when you should have multiplied.

For waves moving at the same speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength. If the frequency doubles, the wavelength is cut in half.

example.prompt: A sound wave has a frequency of 170 Hz and a wavelength of 2.0 m. What is its speed?
example.answer: 340 m/s (a typical speed of sound in air)

check.prompt: An ocean wave has a frequency of 0.20 Hz and a wavelength of 25 m. Use v = f × λ to find its speed in meters per second.

mistakes.why: You divided 25 by 0.20. The formula multiplies: 0.20 × 25 = 5.0 m/s.
You divided 0.20 by 25. Speed is frequency times wavelength: 0.20 × 25 = 5.0 m/s.
You added the two numbers. Speed is frequency multiplied by wavelength: 0.20 × 25 = 5.0 m/s.

check.hint: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.
check.explain:
v = f × λ = 0.20 × 25 = 5.0 m/s

A low frequency (one wave every 5 seconds) with a long wavelength gives a moderate speed.

screens.title: Mechanical waves and the electromagnetic spectrum
screens.html:
Mechanical waves need matter (a medium) to travel through: sound, water waves, earthquake waves. Sound cannot travel through empty space.

Electromagnetic (EM) waves do not need matter. They all travel through space at the speed of light, 3.0 × 108 m/s. The full range of EM waves is the electromagnetic spectrum:

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible (red … violet) → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma ray

Moving right: wavelength gets shorter, frequency gets higher, energy per wave gets higher.

Memory sentence: Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens.

That is why ultraviolet light causes sunburn and X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells, while radio waves pass through you harmlessly.

check.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic wave has a shorter wavelength and more energy than visible light?
options: Ultraviolet
Infrared
Microwaves
Radio waves
why: Infrared sits just before visible light, on the long-wavelength side, so it has a longer wavelength and less energy.
Microwaves come before infrared in the spectrum, so their wavelength is longer than visible light's and their energy is lower.
Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and the least energy in the whole spectrum.
check.hint: Say the memory sentence. Which wave comes right after Visible?
check.explain: In the order radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma, the waves to the right of visible light have shorter wavelengths and more energy. Ultraviolet is the next one to the right. Infrared, microwaves, and radio are all to the left, with longer wavelengths and less energy.

screens.title: Electric circuits
screens.html:
A circuit is a closed loop that electric charges flow around. It needs a source (battery or outlet), wires (conductors), and a load that uses the energy (bulb, motor). An open switch breaks the loop, and the current stops everywhere in that loop.

  • Voltage (V), in volts: the push that moves the charges.
  • Current (I), in amperes (A): how much charge flows each second.
  • Resistance (R), in ohms (Ω): how much the parts oppose the flow.

Series circuit: one path. Resistances add: Rtotal = R1 + R2. If one bulb burns out, the loop is broken and all go out.

Parallel circuit: separate branches. If one bulb burns out, the others stay lit. Homes are wired this way.

check.prompt: A string of decorative lights is wired in series. One bulb burns out. What happens, and why?
options: All the bulbs go out, because the single path for current is broken.
Only that bulb goes out, because each bulb has its own separate path.
The other bulbs get brighter, because the burned-out bulb's energy goes to them.
Nothing changes, because the battery still supplies the same voltage.
why: Separate paths for each bulb describe a parallel circuit. In series there is only one path, so a break anywhere stops all the current.
With the loop broken, no current flows at all, so no bulb can get brighter. Energy is not passed along from a dead bulb.
The battery's voltage cannot push charges through a broken loop. With no complete path, the current stops.
check.hint: How many paths does current have in a series circuit?
check.explain: A series circuit has one path. A burned-out bulb is like a cut in the wire: the loop is open, the current stops, and all the bulbs go out. In a parallel circuit, the other bulbs would stay lit because each has its own path.

screens.title: Ohm's law: V = IR
screens.html:
Ohm’s law connects voltage, current, and resistance.

V = I × R    I = V ÷ R    R = V ÷ I

Triangle trick: draw V on top, I and R on the bottom. Cover the one you want. If the other two are side by side, multiply; if one is over the other, divide.

Key relationship: if the voltage stays the same and the resistance goes up, the current goes down.

For a series circuit, add the resistances first, then use Ohm's law with the total.

example.prompt: A 12 V battery runs a series circuit with a 4.0 Ω and a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find the current.

check.prompt: A current of 0.25 A flows through a 48 Ω resistor. Use V = IR to find the voltage across the resistor, in volts.

mistakes.why: You divided 48 by 0.25. Voltage is current times resistance: 0.25 × 48 = 12 V.
You added current and resistance. Ohm's law multiplies them: V = 0.25 × 48 = 12 V.
You divided 0.25 by 48. To find voltage, multiply: V = I × R = 0.25 × 48 = 12 V.

check.hint: You know I and R. Which form of Ohm's law gives V?
check.explain:
V = I × R = 0.25 × 48 = 12 V

Check with I = V ÷ R: 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 A. It matches.

screens.title: Reading energy and circuit data
screens.html:
Many GED items give you a table or graph and ask which conclusion the data support. Use this routine:

  1. Identify what was changed and what was measured.
  2. Read the measured values in order and describe the trend.
  3. If a formula is given, test it on each row. A value that stays the same in every row (such as V = I × R) is a strong clue.
  4. Reject choices that reverse the trend, go beyond the data, or use words like “always” that the data cannot prove.

A student connected identical bulbs in series to the same 6.0 V battery:

Number of bulbs123
Current (A)0.600.300.20

check.prompt: Use the bulb table on this screen. Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Each bulb has a resistance of about 10 Ω.
Adding bulbs in series raised the total resistance, so the current fell.
Adding bulbs in series made the battery's voltage drop.
Four bulbs in series would carry a current of 0.10 A.
Current increased as more bulbs were added to the circuit.
why: The same 6.0 V battery was used every time. The current fell because the resistance rose, not because the voltage changed.
Four bulbs give R<sub>total</sub> = 4 × 10 = 40 Ω, so I = 6.0 ÷ 40 = 0.15 A, not 0.10 A. The current does not drop by the same amount each time.
Read the table in order: 0.60, 0.30, 0.20 A. The current went down, not up.
check.hint: Use R = V ÷ I on the one-bulb column. What happens to total resistance each time a bulb is added?
check.explain: With one bulb, R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.60 = 10 Ω. Two bulbs in series: 20 Ω, so I = 6.0 ÷ 20 = 0.30 A. Three bulbs: 30 Ω, so I = 0.20 A. Each bulb adds resistance, so the current falls. Four bulbs would give 6.0 ÷ 40 = 0.15 A, so the 0.10 A prediction is wrong; it assumes the current drops by a fixed amount.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Energy (joules): kinetic = motion (including thermal, sound, electrical); potential = stored (gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear); light travels as EM waves.
  • Conservation: energy is never created or destroyed. “Lost” energy became thermal energy through friction. Efficiency = useful out ÷ total in × 100%.
  • KE = ½mv2 (square first; double speed → 4× KE). PE = mgh (g = 9.8). Falling: PE → KE.
  • Heat flows warm → cool: conduction (touch), convection (moving fluid), radiation (EM waves, even through space).
  • Waves carry energy: v = f × λ. Bigger amplitude = more energy. Radio → gamma: shorter λ, higher f, more energy.
  • Circuits: V = IR. Same voltage, more resistance → less current. Series resistances add; one break stops a series circuit.

Routine for every calculation: write the formula, put each number under its letter, calculate one step per line, then check whether your answer is double, half, or a square root of another choice.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.
