items.prompt: A battery-powered flashlight is switched on and shines a beam of light. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions in the flashlight?
options: Chemical energy → electrical energy → light energy
Light energy → electrical energy → chemical energy
Electrical energy → chemical energy → nuclear energy
Thermal energy → chemical energy → light energy
why: This runs backward. Light → electrical → chemical describes a solar charger filling a battery, not a flashlight using one.
A flashlight starts with a battery's stored chemical energy, not electricity, and nothing in it involves nuclear energy.
Thermal energy is a by-product the bulb gives off at the end, not the starting form. The battery's chemical energy comes first.
items.hint: Start with where the energy is stored before the flashlight is turned on.
items.explain:
The battery stores chemical energy. When the switch closes, chemical reactions in the battery push charges through the circuit as electrical energy. The bulb changes the electrical energy into light energy (plus some thermal energy).

The reversed sequence (light → electrical → chemical) describes something like a solar charger filling a battery, not a flashlight in use. Nothing in a flashlight involves nuclear energy, and thermal energy is a by-product, not the starting form.

items.prompt: A cook leaves a metal spoon resting in a pot of simmering soup. A few minutes later, the end of the handle sticking out of the pot feels hot. By which process did thermal energy travel up the handle?
options: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Evaporation
why: Convection needs a moving liquid or gas. It explains how the soup circulates in the pot, not how heat travels through a solid spoon.
Radiation carries energy across a gap as electromagnetic waves. Here the heat travels through the touching metal of the spoon.
Evaporation is a liquid changing to a gas. It is a change of state, not a way heat travels along a spoon.
items.hint: The energy moved through a solid object, from one end to the other.
items.explain:
Heat moved through the solid metal by conduction: particles at the hot end vibrate faster and bump into neighboring particles, passing energy along the spoon to the handle. Metals are good conductors, so this happens quickly.

Convection requires a moving liquid or gas, so it explains how the soup itself circulates, not how heat moves through a solid spoon. Radiation is energy carried by electromagnetic waves across a gap, and evaporation is a change of state, not a way heat travels through a spoon.

items.prompt: Sort each example into the method of heat transfer it shows.
choices: A pan handle gets hot while the pan sits on a burner
Warm air from a floor heater rises and spreads through a room
Sunlight warms the seats of a parked car
You feel the heat of a campfire from several feet away
An ice pack held against your skin makes your skin cooler
Warm water in an ocean current flows north and warms the coast
items.why: The most common wrong placement is putting the ice pack under convection or treating it as cold flowing into the skin. The ice pack touches the skin, so heat leaves the warmer skin by conduction.
items.hint: Touching = conduction. Moving liquid or gas = convection. Waves across a distance = radiation.
items.explain:
• Conduction (direct contact): the pan handle heating up; the ice pack against your skin (heat flows from your warmer skin into the cooler ice pack).
  • Convection (moving fluid): warm air rising and circulating from the heater; the moving ocean current carrying warm water.
  • Radiation (electromagnetic waves): sunlight warming the car seats; feeling a campfire’s heat from a distance. No touching and no moving fluid is needed.

A common mistake is to call the ice pack “cold flowing into the skin.” Heat always flows from warmer to cooler, so your skin loses heat to the ice pack by conduction.

items.prompt: A 60 kg runner is moving at a speed of 5.0 m/s. Kinetic energy can be calculated with the formula KE = ½mv2. What is the runner’s kinetic energy?
why: 150 J is ½ × 60 × 5.0. You forgot to square the speed first: 5.0<sup>2</sup> = 25.
300 J is mass × speed (60 × 5.0), which is the momentum formula, not kinetic energy.
1,500 J is 60 × 25. You squared the speed correctly but forgot to take half.
items.hint: Square the speed before you do anything else.
items.explain:
KE = ½mv2
v2 = 5.0 × 5.0 = 25
60 × 25 = 1,500
½ × 1,500 = 750 J

1,500 J comes from forgetting the ½. 150 J comes from not squaring the speed (½ × 60 × 5). 300 J is just mass × speed, which is not a kinetic energy formula.

items.prompt: Using PE = mgh, calculate the gravitational potential energy of the 0.50 kg pendulum ball when it is held at a release height of 0.80 m. Enter your answer in joules.

mistakes.why: You multiplied only mass and height (0.50 × 0.80). Include g = 9.8: 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.80 = 3.92 J.
You took half of the answer. PE = mgh has no ½; that belongs to kinetic energy. 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.80 = 3.92 J.
7.84 J is the PE at 1.60 m, the next row of the table. The question asks about 0.80 m: 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.80 = 3.92 J.

items.hint: Multiply the mass, 9.8, and the height.
items.explain:
PE = mgh
PE = 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.80
0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9
4.9 × 0.80 = 3.92 J

A common error is to leave out g and multiply only 0.50 × 0.80 = 0.40. The 9.8 m/s2 for gravity must be included.

items.prompt: At every release height, the measured speed was slightly lower than the predicted speed. Which statement best explains this result?
options: Air resistance and friction where the string was attached changed some of the ball’s energy into thermal energy.
Some of the ball’s energy was destroyed by the pull of the string as the ball swung down toward its lowest point.
The ball’s mass increased slightly as it swung downward through the air, which made it move more slowly.
The ball gained extra potential energy as it moved down toward its lowest point, leaving less energy for motion.
why: Energy cannot be destroyed. The law of conservation of energy says it only changes form, so the missing energy must have become another form.
The ball's mass does not change as it swings. And in KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>, more mass would mean more energy, not a lower speed.
Moving down means losing height, so the ball loses potential energy on the way down. It does not gain any.
items.hint: Energy cannot disappear. Ask what other form some of it could have changed into.
items.explain:
The prediction assumed that all of the potential energy would become kinetic energy. In a real pendulum, air pushes against the moving ball and the string rubs where it is attached. These forces change a small amount of the energy into thermal energy (and a little sound), so less kinetic energy is left and the ball moves slightly slower.

“Energy was destroyed” is wrong because the law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be destroyed, only changed in form. The ball’s mass does not change, and the ball loses potential energy as it moves down; it does not gain any.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the cup-wrapping experiment.

The water in every mug cooled because thermal energy flowed from {{0}}. Over the 30 minutes, the mug wrapped in {{1}} lost the least thermal energy, so that material was the best {{2}} in the test.

options: the warmer water to the cooler room air
the cooler room air to the warmer water
the wrapping material into the water
the table into the water
why: Heat never flows from cooler to warmer on its own. The water (80 °C) was warmer than the room (22 °C), so heat left the water.
The wrapping did not supply heat; it only slowed the heat leaving. The water was the warm object losing thermal energy.
The table was at room temperature, cooler than the water, so heat could not flow from the table into the water.

options: no wrap
aluminum foil
a wool sock
a foam sleeve
why: The unwrapped mug dropped the most (80 − 48 = 32 °C). It lost the most thermal energy, not the least.
Foil dropped 80 − 56 = 24 °C, more than wool or foam. You may have compared it only to the unwrapped mug.
Wool dropped 13 °C, but foam dropped only 80 − 71 = 9 °C, so foam lost less.

options: insulator
conductor
radiator
why: A conductor speeds up heat transfer. The foam slowed it, which makes foam an insulator.
Radiation is a way heat travels, not a type of material. A material that slows heat transfer is an insulator.

items.hint: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Find the mug whose temperature dropped the fewest degrees.
items.explain:
The water started at 80 °C and the room was 22 °C, so heat flowed from the warmer water to the cooler room air. Heat never flows from cooler to warmer on its own.

Temperature drops over 30 minutes: no wrap 80 − 48 = 32 °C; foil 80 − 56 = 24 °C; wool 80 − 67 = 13 °C; foam 80 − 71 = 9 °C. The foam sleeve mug cooled the least, so foam slowed heat transfer the most. A material that slows heat transfer is an insulator; a conductor would speed it up.

items.prompt: A sound wave traveling through air has a frequency of 250 Hz and a wavelength of 1.36 m. Wave speed can be found with v = f × λ. What is the speed of the sound wave?
why: 0.0054 m/s comes from dividing 1.36 by 250. Wave speed is frequency times wavelength.
183.8 m/s comes from dividing 250 by 1.36. The formula multiplies: v = f × λ.
251.36 m/s comes from adding the frequency and the wavelength. The formula multiplies them.
items.hint: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.
items.explain:
v = f × λ
v = 250 × 1.36
250 × 1 = 250 and 250 × 0.36 = 90
250 + 90 = 340 m/s

183.8 m/s comes from dividing 250 by 1.36, and 0.0054 m/s comes from dividing 1.36 by 250. 251.36 m/s comes from adding the two numbers. The formula calls for multiplying. (340 m/s is a typical speed of sound in air, which is a good check.)

items.prompt: Which list places these types of electromagnetic waves in order from lowest frequency to highest frequency?
options: Radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays
X-rays, visible light, microwaves, radio waves
Visible light, radio waves, X-rays, microwaves
Microwaves, radio waves, X-rays, visible light
why: This list runs from highest to lowest frequency, exactly backward. X-rays have the highest frequency of these four.
Visible light has a higher frequency than radio waves, so it cannot come first. Radio waves have the lowest frequency.
Radio waves have a lower frequency than microwaves, so radio must come first. Visible light also belongs before X-rays.
items.hint: Radio waves have the longest wavelength. Longest wavelength means lowest frequency.
items.explain:
The electromagnetic spectrum, from longest wavelength (lowest frequency) to shortest wavelength (highest frequency), is: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. So the correct order is radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays.

The choice beginning with X-rays lists the waves from highest to lowest frequency; it is exactly backward. The other two choices mix up the order.

items.prompt: The student uses the same battery with a new 12 Ω resistor. Based on the data and Ohm’s law, what current, in amperes, should she measure?

mistakes.why: 108 is 9.0 × 12, voltage times resistance. To find current, divide: I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A.
You divided 12 by 9.0. Current is voltage divided by resistance: 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A.
1.0 A is the current for the 9.0 Ω resistor in the table. First find the battery voltage (9.0 V), then divide by the new resistance: 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A.

items.hint: First use any row of the table to find the battery’s voltage with V = IR.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find the battery voltage. Use any row, for example 3.0 A and 3.0 Ω:
V = I × R = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 V
(Check: 1.5 × 6.0 = 9.0, 1.0 × 9.0 = 9.0, 0.50 × 18 = 9.0.)

Step 2: Find the new current.
I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A

A common error is to skip Step 1 or to assume current goes up with resistance. Ohm’s law shows that at the same voltage, more resistance gives less current.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Doubling the resistance from 9.0 Ω to 18 Ω cut the current in half.
For every trial, current × resistance equals 9.0, so the battery supplied about 9.0 V.
Current is directly proportional to resistance.
Increasing the resistance increased the current.
A 36 Ω resistor with the same battery would carry a current of 0.50 A.
why: Directly proportional would mean current rises when resistance rises. In the data, current falls as resistance rises.
Read the table in order: as resistance went from 3.0 to 18 Ω, current fell from 3.0 A to 0.50 A. It did not increase.
0.50 A is the current for 18 Ω. For 36 Ω, I = 9.0 ÷ 36 = 0.25 A. Doubling resistance halves the current again.
items.hint: Multiply the current by the resistance in each row. What do you notice?
items.explain:
Supported:

  • At 9.0 Ω the current was 1.0 A; at 18 Ω it was 0.50 A. Doubling the resistance halved the current.
  • 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0; 1.5 × 6.0 = 9.0; 1.0 × 9.0 = 9.0; 0.50 × 18 = 9.0. Since V = IR, the battery voltage was 9.0 V each time.

Not supported: Current went down as resistance went up, so it is not directly proportional and it did not increase. A 36 Ω resistor would carry I = 9.0 ÷ 36 = 0.25 A, not 0.50 A.

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignore air resistance. Use PE = mgh (g = 9.8 m/s2) and KE = ½mv2. Assuming all of the ball’s potential energy changes into kinetic energy, what is its speed just before it hits the ground?
why: 14.0 m/s comes from leaving out the ½: 392 = 2.0 × v<sup>2</sup>, so v<sup>2</sup> = 196 and v = 14.0. With the ½, v<sup>2</sup> = 392.
196 m/s comes from leaving out the ½ and also forgetting the square root. Use 392 = ½ × 2.0 × v<sup>2</sup>, then take √392.
392 m/s is v<sup>2</sup>, not v. You found v<sup>2</sup> = 392 correctly but forgot to take the square root.
items.hint: Find the PE at the top first. Set that equal to KE, then solve for v. Do not forget the square root.
items.explain:
Step 1: PE at the top. PE = 2.0 × 9.8 × 20 = 392 J.

Step 2: Set KE equal to PE. 392 = ½ × 2.0 × v2
½ × 2.0 = 1.0, so 392 = 1.0 × v2
v2 = 392

Step 3: Take the square root. v = √392 ≈ 19.8 m/s

392 m/s comes from forgetting the square root. 14.0 m/s and 196 m/s come from leaving out the ½ in the KE formula (v2 = 392 ÷ 2.0 = 196, so v = 14.0, or 196 if the square root is also skipped).

items.prompt: All three bulbs give off the same amount of visible light. Which statement best explains why the incandescent bulb uses 60 J each second while the LED uses only 10 J?
options: The incandescent bulb changes most of its electrical energy into thermal energy instead of light.
The incandescent bulb destroys most of its electrical energy before any light is produced.
The incandescent bulb gives off much more visible light energy each second than the LED.
The LED bulb creates extra light energy that does not come from the electricity it uses.
why: Energy cannot be destroyed. The table shows where the incandescent bulb's energy goes: 55.8 J of thermal energy each second.
The table shows 4.2 J of visible light each second for every bulb. The light output is the same; the difference is thermal energy.
Energy cannot be created. The LED's 4.2 J of light comes from its 10 J of electrical energy; it simply wastes less as heat.
items.hint: Compare the light column and the thermal energy column for the incandescent bulb.
items.explain:
Each bulb gives off 4.2 J of visible light per second. The incandescent bulb uses 60 J, so 60 − 4.2 = 55.8 J becomes thermal energy, which is why these bulbs get hot. The LED wastes only 5.8 J as heat. Energy is conserved in every bulb: light + thermal = electrical energy used.

The idea that the incandescent bulb gives off more light is tempting, but the table shows the same 4.2 J for all three.

items.prompt: What is the efficiency of the compact fluorescent (CFL) bulb at producing visible light? Enter your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: 70% is the share that became thermal energy (9.8 ÷ 14). Efficiency uses the useful energy, the light: 4.2 ÷ 14 × 100 = 30%.
You divided the total by the useful energy (14 ÷ 4.2). Put the useful energy on top: 4.2 ÷ 14 = 0.30 = 30%.
7% is the incandescent bulb's efficiency (4.2 ÷ 60). The question asks about the CFL: 4.2 ÷ 14 × 100 = 30%.

items.hint: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%. The useful energy is the light.
items.explain:
Useful energy out (light) = 4.2 J. Total energy in = 14 J.
4.2 ÷ 14 = 0.30
0.30 × 100% = 30%

The other 70% (9.8 J) became thermal energy. Putting 14 on top gives a number over 100%, which is impossible for efficiency.

items.prompt: Waves P and Q travel along the same rope at the same speed. The diagram shows both waves at one instant. Wave speed is given by v = f × λ. Which statement is correct?

figure.alt: Two waves drawn over a distance scale from 0 to 4 meters, with the same height. Wave P completes one full cycle every 2 meters. Wave Q completes one full cycle every 1 meter.

options: Wave Q has twice the frequency of wave P.
Wave Q travels twice as fast as wave P.
Wave Q has twice the wavelength of wave P.
Wave Q has the larger amplitude of the two.
why: The problem states both waves travel at the same speed. Q has more waves packed into the same distance, which means a higher frequency, not a higher speed.
Read the scale: P repeats every 2 m and Q repeats every 1 m. Q has half the wavelength of P, not twice.
Both waves rise and fall the same height above and below the rest line, so their amplitudes are equal.
items.hint: Read each wavelength from the scale. If v stays the same, what must happen to f when λ is cut in half?
items.explain:
From the scale, wave P repeats every 2 m and wave Q every 1 m. Both have the same speed, so f × λ is the same for both. Q's wavelength is half of P's, so Q's frequency must be twice P's. For example, if v = 4 m/s, then fP = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 Hz and fQ = 4 ÷ 1 = 4 Hz.

The tempting wrong idea is that the “busier” wave Q moves faster. On the same rope, the speed is the same; Q just has more waves per second.

items.prompt: A wind turbine on a hill sends electricity to a power line. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions in the turbine?
options: Kinetic energy of the wind → kinetic energy of the blades → electrical energy
Electrical energy → kinetic energy of the blades → kinetic energy of the wind
Chemical energy of fuel → thermal energy → electrical energy
Light energy from the Sun → electrical energy → kinetic energy of the blades
why: This runs backward. Electricity spinning blades to push air describes a fan, not a turbine making electricity.
A wind turbine burns no fuel. This chain describes a power plant that burns coal or gas.
This describes a solar panel running a motor. A wind turbine's energy comes from moving air, and electricity is what it produces at the end.
items.hint: Start with what pushes the blades. What does the turbine produce at the end?
items.explain: Moving air has kinetic energy. The wind pushes the blades, giving them kinetic energy as they spin. A generator inside the turbine changes that motion into electrical energy (with some thermal energy and sound given off). The reversed chain describes a fan.

items.prompt: A pot of water is heated on a stove. The water at the bottom warms and rises, and cooler water from the top sinks to take its place. The water keeps circulating in a loop. By which process is thermal energy moving through the water?
options: Convection
Conduction
Radiation
Insulation
why: Conduction is transfer by direct contact without the material flowing. Here the warm water itself moves and carries the heat.
Radiation is energy carried by electromagnetic waves across a gap. The description is about water moving in a loop.
Insulation is slowing heat transfer with a material such as foam. It is not a way heat moves.
items.hint: Is a liquid or gas moving and carrying the heat with it?
items.explain: Warm water is less dense, so it rises; cooler water sinks. This circulating loop is a convection current, and it carries thermal energy through the pot. (Heat does reach the bottom water from the hot pot by conduction, but the circulation described is convection.)

items.prompt: Sort each example into the method of heat transfer it shows.
choices: A metal seat-belt buckle in a hot car burns your hand when you touch it
A heat lamp at a restaurant keeps plates of food warm from above
Warm air from a wall heater rises and circulates around a bedroom
Your bare feet feel cold on a tile floor in the morning
On a sunny afternoon, cool air from the ocean moves in as warm air over the land rises
Standing in sunshine on a cold day warms your face
items.why: The most common wrong placement is the tile floor. Nothing cold flows into your feet; heat leaves your warmer feet and moves into the cooler tile by direct contact, which is conduction.
items.hint: Touching = conduction. Moving liquid or gas = convection. Waves across a distance = radiation.
items.explain:
• Conduction (direct contact): the hot buckle against your hand; your feet on the tile (heat flows from your warmer feet into the cooler floor).
  • Convection (moving fluid): warm air rising and circulating from the heater; the sea breeze, where rising warm air over land pulls in cooler ocean air.
  • Radiation (electromagnetic waves): the heat lamp warming food from above; sunshine warming your face. Nothing touches and no fluid carries the heat.

items.prompt: An 80 kg cyclist is moving at a speed of 6.0 m/s. Kinetic energy can be calculated with the formula KE = ½mv2. What is the cyclist’s kinetic energy?
why: 240 J is ½ × 80 × 6.0. You forgot to square the speed: 6.0<sup>2</sup> = 36.
480 J is mass × speed (80 × 6.0), which is momentum, not kinetic energy.
2,880 J is 80 × 36. You squared the speed but forgot to take half.
items.hint: Square the speed before you do anything else.
items.explain:
KE = ½mv2
v2 = 6.0 × 6.0 = 36
80 × 36 = 2,880
½ × 2,880 = 1,440 J

2,880 J comes from forgetting the ½. 240 J comes from not squaring the speed. 480 J is mass × speed.

items.prompt: Using PE = mgh, calculate the gravitational potential energy of the 1.5 kg cart when it is held at a release height of 0.40 m. Enter your answer in joules.

mistakes.why: You multiplied only mass and height (1.5 × 0.40). Include g = 9.8: 1.5 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 5.88 J.
You took half of the answer. PE = mgh has no ½. 1.5 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 5.88 J.
11.76 J is the PE at 0.80 m, the next row. The question asks about 0.40 m: 1.5 × 9.8 × 0.40 = 5.88 J.

items.hint: Multiply the mass, 9.8, and the height.
items.explain:
PE = mgh
PE = 1.5 × 9.8 × 0.40
1.5 × 9.8 = 14.7
14.7 × 0.40 = 5.88 J

A common error is to leave out g and get 0.60. The 9.8 m/s2 for gravity must be included.

items.prompt: At every release height, the cart’s measured speed was lower than the predicted speed. Which statement best explains this result?
options: Friction between the wheels and ramp and air resistance changed some energy into thermal energy.
Part of the cart’s potential energy disappeared completely because the ramp was made of wood.
The cart lost some of its mass as it rolled down the ramp, so it ended with less kinetic energy.
The cart picked up extra potential energy on the way down, so less energy was left for motion.
why: Energy does not disappear. The law of conservation of energy says it changes form, so the missing energy became something else, mostly thermal energy.
The cart's mass stays 1.5 kg the whole time. Nothing in the setup removes mass from the cart.
Rolling down means losing height, so the cart loses potential energy on the way down; it does not gain any.
items.hint: Energy cannot disappear. What form could some of it have changed into?
items.explain:
The prediction assumed all of the potential energy became kinetic energy. In a real ramp, the wheels rub on their axles and on the ramp, and air pushes against the cart. These forces change some energy into thermal energy (and a little sound), so less kinetic energy is left and the cart moves more slowly.

“Disappeared completely” breaks the law of conservation of energy, which is why it is wrong.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the lunch-bag experiment.

The juice in every bottle warmed up because thermal energy flowed from {{0}}. Over the 45 minutes, the juice in the {{1}} gained the least thermal energy, so that material was the best {{2}} in the test.

options: the warmer room air to the cooler juice
the cooler juice to the warmer room air
the cold juice into the bag material
the plastic bottle into the room air
why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler. The juice (4 °C) was cooler than the room (24 °C), so heat flowed into the juice, which is why it warmed up.
If heat left the juice, the juice would get colder, but it warmed up. Heat flowed into the juice from the warmer room.
Heat leaving the bottle would cool the juice, but the juice warmed. Heat moved from the room air toward the juice.

options: bottle with no bag
paper bag
cloth bag
foam-lined bag
why: The unwrapped bottle warmed the most (19 − 4 = 15 °C). It gained the most thermal energy, not the least.
The paper bag juice warmed 16 − 4 = 12 °C, more than the cloth or foam-lined bag.
The cloth bag juice warmed 10 °C, but the foam-lined bag juice warmed only 8 − 4 = 4 °C.

options: insulator
conductor
radiator
why: A conductor lets heat through easily. The foam lining slowed heat transfer, which makes it an insulator.
Radiation is a way heat travels, not a kind of material. A material that slows heat transfer is an insulator.

items.hint: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Find the bottle whose temperature rose the fewest degrees.
items.explain:
The juice started at 4 °C in a 24 °C room, so heat flowed from the warmer room air into the cooler juice. That is why every bottle warmed.

Temperature rises over 45 minutes: no bag 19 − 4 = 15 °C; paper 16 − 4 = 12 °C; cloth 14 − 4 = 10 °C; foam-lined 8 − 4 = 4 °C. The foam-lined bag slowed heat transfer the most, so foam is the best insulator. Insulators keep cold things cold for the same reason they keep hot things hot: they slow heat flow in either direction.

items.prompt: Ocean waves approaching a beach have a frequency of 0.10 Hz and a wavelength of 40 m. Wave speed can be found with v = f × λ. What is the speed of the waves?
why: 0.0025 m/s comes from dividing 0.10 by 40. Wave speed is frequency times wavelength.
40.1 m/s comes from adding the frequency and the wavelength. The formula multiplies them.
400 m/s comes from dividing 40 by 0.10. The formula multiplies: 0.10 × 40 = 4.0.
items.hint: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.
items.explain:
v = f × λ
v = 0.10 × 40 = 4.0 m/s

400 m/s comes from dividing instead of multiplying. Check the units: Hz is “per second,” so (1/s) × m = m/s.

items.prompt: Which list places these types of electromagnetic waves in order from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength?
options: Microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays
Gamma rays, ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves
Infrared, microwaves, gamma rays, ultraviolet
Ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves, gamma rays
why: This list runs from shortest to longest, exactly backward. Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength of all.
Microwaves have longer wavelengths than infrared, so they come first; and ultraviolet comes before gamma rays.
Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength than infrared and microwaves, so it cannot be first. Microwaves are the longest here.
items.hint: Use the memory sentence. Waves earlier in the spectrum have longer wavelengths.
items.explain: The spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. So the correct order is microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays. The list starting with gamma rays is the same order reversed.

items.prompt: The student sets the power supply to 9.0 V and uses the same resistor. Based on the data and Ohm’s law, what current, in amperes, should she measure?

mistakes.why: 45 is 9.0 × 5.0, voltage times resistance. To find current, divide: I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 5.0 = 1.8 A.
You divided resistance by voltage (5.0 ÷ 9.0). Current is voltage divided by resistance: 9.0 ÷ 5.0 = 1.8 A.
You may have added 0.30 A once to the 6.0 V current. From 6.0 V to 9.0 V is two steps of 1.5 V, so add 0.30 A twice: 1.20 + 0.60 = 1.8 A.

items.hint: First use any row of the table to find the resistance with R = V ÷ I.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find the resistance. Use any row, for example 3.0 V and 0.60 A:
R = V ÷ I = 3.0 ÷ 0.60 = 5.0 Ω
(Check: 1.5 ÷ 0.30 = 5.0, 4.5 ÷ 0.90 = 5.0, 6.0 ÷ 1.20 = 5.0.)

Step 2: Find the new current.
I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 5.0 = 1.8 A

Check with the pattern: every 1.5 V adds 0.30 A, and 9.0 V is 6 steps of 1.5 V, so 6 × 0.30 = 1.8 A.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Doubling the voltage from 3.0 V to 6.0 V doubled the current.
For every trial, voltage ÷ current equals 5.0, so the resistor is about 5.0 Ω.
Current decreased as the voltage increased.
Current is inversely proportional to voltage.
A 12 V supply would push a current of 3.0 A through this resistor.
why: Read the table in order: as voltage rose from 1.5 V to 6.0 V, current rose from 0.30 A to 1.20 A. It increased.
Inversely proportional means one goes up as the other goes down. Here both rise together, so current is directly proportional to voltage.
At 12 V, I = 12 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4 A, not 3.0 A. Doubling 6.0 V to 12 V doubles 1.20 A to 2.4 A.
items.hint: Divide the voltage by the current in each row. What do you notice?
items.explain:
Supported:

  • At 3.0 V the current was 0.60 A; at 6.0 V it was 1.20 A. Doubling the voltage doubled the current.
  • 1.5 ÷ 0.30 = 5.0; 3.0 ÷ 0.60 = 5.0; 4.5 ÷ 0.90 = 5.0; 6.0 ÷ 1.20 = 5.0. Since R = V ÷ I, the resistance is 5.0 Ω.

Not supported: Current went up with voltage, so it did not decrease and is not inversely proportional. At 12 V, the current would be 12 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4 A, not 3.0 A.

items.prompt: A 4.0 kg rock falls from rest off a ledge 45 m high. Ignore air resistance. Use PE = mgh (g = 9.8 m/s2) and KE = ½mv2. Assuming all of the rock’s potential energy changes into kinetic energy, what is its speed just before it hits the ground?
why: 21.0 m/s comes from leaving out the ½: 1,764 = 4.0 × v<sup>2</sup> gives v<sup>2</sup> = 441 and v = 21.0. With the ½, v<sup>2</sup> = 882.
441 m/s comes from leaving out the ½ and also skipping the square root.
882 m/s is v<sup>2</sup>, not v. You found v<sup>2</sup> = 882 correctly but forgot to take the square root.
items.hint: Find the PE at the top first. Set that equal to KE, then solve for v. Do not forget the square root.
items.explain:
Step 1: PE at the top. PE = 4.0 × 9.8 × 45 = 1,764 J.

Step 2: Set KE equal to PE. 1,764 = ½ × 4.0 × v2
½ × 4.0 = 2.0, so 1,764 = 2.0 × v2
v2 = 1,764 ÷ 2.0 = 882

Step 3: Take the square root. v = √882 ≈ 29.7 m/s

882 m/s comes from forgetting the square root. 21.0 m/s and 441 m/s come from leaving out the ½.

items.prompt: All three appliances gave the water the same 160,000 J of thermal energy. Which statement best explains why the microwave oven used the most electrical energy?
options: More of the microwave’s energy went into forms other than heating the water, such as warming its parts and the air.
The microwave destroyed part of its electrical energy before the energy could reach the water.
The water in the microwave oven absorbed more thermal energy than the water in the kettle.
The kettle created extra thermal energy, so it needed less electrical energy than the microwave.
why: Energy cannot be destroyed. The 160,000 J the microwave did not deliver to the water still exists, mostly as thermal energy in the oven and the air.
The table shows every appliance gave the water about 160,000 J. The water's energy was the same; the difference is in the energy used.
Energy cannot be created. The kettle needed less electricity because less of its energy was wasted, not because it made extra energy.
items.hint: The useful energy is the same for all three. Where did the rest of each appliance's energy go?
items.explain:
Each appliance gave the water 160,000 J. The microwave used 320,000 J, so 320,000 − 160,000 = 160,000 J went into other forms: thermal energy in the oven's parts and the surrounding air, light, and sound. The kettle wasted only 40,000 J. That makes the microwave the least efficient (50%) and the kettle the most efficient (80%).

The water did not absorb more energy in the microwave; the table shows the same 160,000 J in every case.

items.prompt: What is the efficiency of heating the water in a pot on the electric stovetop burner? Enter your answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: 36% is the share of energy that did not go into the water (90,000 ÷ 250,000). Efficiency uses the useful energy: 160,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 64%.
You divided the total by the useful energy (250,000 ÷ 160,000). Put the useful energy on top: 160,000 ÷ 250,000 = 0.64 = 64%.
90,000 J is the energy that went into other forms (250,000 − 160,000). Efficiency is a percent: 160,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 64%.

items.hint: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%. The useful energy is what the water absorbed.
items.explain:
Useful energy out (water) = 160,000 J. Total energy in = 250,000 J.
160,000 ÷ 250,000 = 0.64
0.64 × 100% = 64%

The other 36% (90,000 J) warmed the burner, the pot, and the kitchen air. Putting 250,000 on top gives over 100%, which is impossible for efficiency.

items.prompt: A keyboard plays a note at 220 Hz, then a higher note at 440 Hz. Both sound waves travel through the same room air at 343 m/s. Using v = f × λ, which statement correctly describes the change?
options: The wavelength decreases from about 1.56 m to about 0.78 m.
The wavelength increases from about 0.78 m to about 1.56 m.
The wavelength stays about 1.56 m, and the speed doubles to 686 m/s.
The wavelength decreases from about 1.56 m to about 0.39 m.
why: You have the direction reversed. A higher frequency at the same speed means a shorter wavelength: 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m.
Sound travels at the same speed in the same air no matter the pitch. The speed stays 343 m/s, so the wavelength must change instead.
0.39 m would be one quarter of 1.56 m, as if the change were squared. Wavelength is simply v ÷ f: 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m, one half.
items.hint: The speed does not change. Find λ = v ÷ f for each note.
items.explain:
λ = v ÷ f
At 220 Hz: 343 ÷ 220 ≈ 1.56 m
At 440 Hz: 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m

Doubling the frequency at the same speed cuts the wavelength in half. The tempting wrong idea is that a higher note travels faster; in the same air, all sounds travel at the same speed.

items.prompt: A pole vaulter sprints down the runway, plants a flexible pole, and the pole bends deeply. As the pole straightens, it lifts the vaulter high over the bar. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions?
options: Kinetic energy → elastic potential energy → gravitational potential energy
Gravitational potential energy → elastic potential energy → kinetic energy
Kinetic energy → chemical energy → gravitational potential energy
Elastic potential energy → kinetic energy → thermal energy
why: This runs backward. The vaulter starts low and moving fast and ends up high, so the chain must end with gravitational potential energy, not start with it.
The bent pole stores energy by being bent, which is elastic potential energy, not chemical energy. Nothing burns or reacts in the pole.
The pole is not bent at the start; the running vaulter bends it. And the goal of the vault is height, so the chain ends with gravitational potential energy.
items.explain: The sprinting vaulter has kinetic energy. Planting the pole bends it, storing that energy as elastic potential energy. As the pole straightens, it lifts the vaulter, turning the stored energy into gravitational potential energy at the top. The reversed chain describes the fall back down, not the rise.

items.prompt: A 1,000 kg car travels at 20 m/s. Use KE = ½mv2 to find its kinetic energy in joules.

mistakes.why: 400,000 is 1,000 × 400. You squared the speed but forgot to take half: 400,000 ÷ 2 = 200,000 J.
You did not square the speed: ½ × 1,000 × 20 = 10,000. Square first: 20<sup>2</sup> = 400.
20,000 is mass × speed, which is momentum, not kinetic energy. Use ½ × m × v<sup>2</sup>.

items.explain:
v2 = 20 × 20 = 400
1,000 × 400 = 400,000
400,000 ÷ 2 = 200,000 J

400,000 J would mean the ½ was left out.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The car’s total energy (PE + KE) decreased from point A to point D.
Between points A and B, about 7,840 J changed into other forms, such as thermal energy and sound.
At point C, the car had more kinetic energy than potential energy.
Friction destroyed some of the car’s energy as it moved along the track.
The car’s kinetic energy was greatest at point D, the end of the ride.
why: At point C, KE was 66,400 J and PE was 78,400 J. The car had more potential energy than kinetic energy there.
Energy cannot be destroyed. Friction changed some of it into thermal energy and sound, which is why PE + KE went down.
KE was 148,960 J at point B but only 140,000 J at point D. It was greatest at the bottom of the first hill.
items.explain:
Add PE + KE at each point: A = 156,800 J; B = 148,960 J; C = 78,400 + 66,400 = 144,800 J; D = 140,000 J. The total decreased steadily. Between A and B: 156,800 − 148,960 = 7,840 J changed into other forms. That energy was not destroyed; friction and air resistance changed it into thermal energy and sound.

At C, PE (78,400 J) is larger than KE (66,400 J). KE peaked at B (148,960 J), not D.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

On a cold day, Ana wraps her hands around a mug of hot cocoa. Thermal energy flows from {{0}} by {{1}}. Inside the mug, warm cocoa near the bottom rises while cooler cocoa sinks, which moves heat through the cocoa by {{2}}.

options: the mug into her hands
her hands into the mug
the cold air into her hands
why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler. The hot mug is warmer than her cold hands, so heat flows from the mug to her hands.
Cold does not flow. The cold air actually takes heat away from her hands; the mug is what warms them.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: Her hands touch the mug directly; nothing is flowing between them. Direct contact is conduction.
Her hands are touching the mug, so the main transfer is by contact. Radiation carries energy across a gap.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: The cocoa itself is moving in a loop, carrying heat with it. A moving liquid or gas is convection.
The heat is carried by the cocoa moving up and down, not by waves crossing a gap. That is convection.

items.explain: The mug is warmer than Ana's hands, so heat flows from the mug into her hands. Because they touch, this is conduction. Inside the mug, warm cocoa rises and cool cocoa sinks, a circulating current: convection.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Copper conducted heat the fastest of the four materials, and wood conducted it the slowest.
Wood is the best conductor of the four, because its far end stayed the coolest.
Heat flowed from the room air into each rod, which then warmed the water in the pan.
Steel would make a cooler pot handle than wood, because steel stayed under 40 °C.
why: A cool far end means little heat got through, so wood is the poorest conductor, an insulator. Good conductors get hot fast, like copper.
The water (90 °C) was warmer than the room (22 °C), so heat flowed from the water through the rods, not from the room into them.
Steel's far end reached 34 °C, but wood's reached only 23 °C. Wood stayed cooler, so it would make the cooler handle.
items.explain:
All rods started at 22 °C with one end in 90 °C water. The far end of the copper rod rose the most (to 62 °C), so copper carried heat through itself the fastest. Wood barely warmed (23 °C), so it conducted heat the slowest; it is an insulator. That is why many pot handles are made of wood or plastic.

The tempting wrong idea is that the coolest rod is the best conductor. It is the reverse: a good conductor lets heat reach the far end quickly.

items.prompt: A tuning fork vibrates at 440 Hz and produces a sound wave with a wavelength of 0.78 m in air. Use v = f × λ to find the speed of the sound, in meters per second.

mistakes.why: You divided 440 by 0.78. The formula multiplies: 440 × 0.78 = 343.2 m/s.
You added the frequency and the wavelength. Speed is frequency times wavelength: 440 × 0.78 = 343.2 m/s.
You divided 0.78 by 440. Multiply instead: v = 440 × 0.78 = 343.2 m/s.

items.explain:
v = f × λ = 440 × 0.78 = 343.2 m/s

That matches the usual speed of sound in room-temperature air (about 343 m/s), a good check.

items.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic wave has a higher frequency than visible light but a lower frequency than X-rays?
options: Ultraviolet
Infrared
Gamma rays
Microwaves
why: Infrared is just below visible light, so its frequency is lower than visible light's, not higher.
Gamma rays are past X-rays at the far end of the spectrum, so their frequency is higher than X-rays'.
Microwaves are on the low-frequency side of the spectrum, below infrared and visible light.
items.explain: Low to high frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. The only type between visible light and X-rays is ultraviolet.

items.prompt: A 24 V battery is connected in a series circuit with a 5.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor. Using V = IR, what is the current in the circuit, in amperes?

mistakes.why: You used only the 5.0 Ω resistor. In series, add the resistances first: 5.0 + 3.0 = 8.0 Ω, then 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 A.
You used only the 3.0 Ω resistor (or stopped at the total resistance, 8.0 Ω). Current = 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 A.
192 is 24 × 8.0. To find current, divide voltage by resistance: 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 A.

items.explain:
Series: Rtotal = 5.0 + 3.0 = 8.0 Ω
I = V ÷ R = 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 A

Using only one resistor gives 4.8 A or 8.0 A; both resistors are in the single loop.

items.prompt: During a power outage, a man turns the crank on an emergency radio. The crank spins a small generator, and the radio plays the news. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions?
options: Kinetic energy → electrical energy → sound energy
Sound energy → electrical energy → kinetic energy
Chemical energy → light energy → sound energy
Electrical energy → kinetic energy → chemical energy
why: This runs backward. The radio produces sound at the end; it does not start with sound.
There is no battery or fuel in this chain, and no light is involved. The energy starts as the motion of the turning crank.
The power is out, so the radio cannot start with electricity from the wall. The crank's motion makes the electricity.
items.explain: Turning the crank gives it kinetic energy. The generator changes that motion into electrical energy. The radio's speaker changes electrical energy into sound energy (with some thermal energy given off). The reversed chain describes something like a microphone powering a motor.

items.prompt: A 0.40 kg soccer ball is kicked at 15 m/s. Use KE = ½mv2 to find its kinetic energy in joules.

mistakes.why: 90 is 0.40 × 225. You squared the speed but forgot to take half: 90 ÷ 2 = 45 J.
You did not square the speed: ½ × 0.40 × 15 = 3. Square first: 15<sup>2</sup> = 225.
6 is mass × speed (0.40 × 15), which is momentum, not kinetic energy. Use ½ × m × v<sup>2</sup>.

items.explain:
v2 = 15 × 15 = 225
0.40 × 225 = 90
90 ÷ 2 = 45 J

90 J would mean the ½ was left out.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: As the skier went downhill, her potential energy decreased while her kinetic energy increased.
From point A to point D, 3,400 J changed into other forms, such as thermal energy from friction.
At point B, the skier had more kinetic energy than potential energy.
The skier’s total energy (PE + KE) stayed exactly the same at every point.
Friction with the snow created new energy, so the skier was fastest at the bottom.
why: At point B, KE was 12,700 J and PE was 20,580 J. She had more potential energy than kinetic energy there.
Add PE + KE: 34,300 J at A but 33,280 J at B, 32,100 J at C, and 30,900 J at D. The total went down, because some energy changed into thermal energy.
Friction does not create energy; it changes kinetic energy into thermal energy and slows the skier. She was fastest at the bottom because she had lost the most height.
items.explain:
Reading down the table, PE falls (34,300 → 20,580 → 6,860 → 0 J) while KE rises (0 → 12,700 → 25,240 → 30,900 J). Starting total = 34,300 J; final total = 30,900 J; 34,300 − 30,900 = 3,400 J changed into other forms, mostly thermal energy from friction with the snow and air resistance.

At B, PE (20,580 J) is larger than KE (12,700 J). The total did not stay the same, and friction never creates energy.

Complete the statements.

A cook holds her hands a few inches above a glowing stovetop burner without touching it. Her hands are warmed by infrared waves from the burner by {{0}}, and also by heated air that rises from the burner by {{1}}. When she grabs the metal handle of a hot pot, thermal energy flows from {{2}}.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: Her hands are not touching the burner, so it cannot be conduction. Infrared waves crossing a gap are radiation.
Convection is heat carried by moving air. The infrared waves themselves carry energy across the gap, which is radiation.

options: conduction
convection
radiation
why: The air is not a solid she touches; it moves upward and carries heat to her hands. Moving air means convection.
The heat in this part is carried by air rising and moving, not by waves. That is convection.

options: the handle into her hand
her hand into the handle
the cool air into the handle

items.explain: Infrared waves from the glowing burner cross the gap to her hands: radiation. Air heated by the burner rises and carries heat upward: convection. The hot handle is warmer than her hand, so heat flows from the handle into her hand by conduction.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The black covering absorbed the most radiant energy from the sunlight, so its water warmed the most.
The silver foil absorbed the most energy, because shiny surfaces draw sunlight toward them.
The cans warmed mainly by conduction from the cooler air that surrounded them on the table.
The covering made no real difference, because every can sat in exactly the same amount of sunlight.
why: The silver can warmed the least, only 4 °C. Shiny surfaces reflect most sunlight, so they absorb the least energy.
Heat flows from warmer to cooler, so cool air cannot warm the cans. The energy came from sunlight, which is radiation.
Same sunlight, but different results: from 24 °C to 41 °C. That 17-degree spread shows the covering made a large difference.
items.explain:
All cans started at 20 °C in the same sunlight. Temperature rises: black 21 °C, red 13 °C, white 6 °C, silver 4 °C. Sunlight reaches the cans by radiation, and dark surfaces absorb more of it while light and shiny surfaces reflect more. So the black can absorbed the most radiant energy.

The tempting wrong idea is that shiny foil “attracts” sunlight; it reflects it, which is why the foil can stayed coolest.

items.prompt: A sound wave travels through air at 340 m/s with a frequency of 680 Hz. Use v = f × λ to find its wavelength, in meters.

mistakes.why: You divided frequency by speed (680 ÷ 340). Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency: 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m.
You multiplied speed by frequency. To find wavelength, rearrange: λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m.
You added the two numbers. Rearrange v = f × λ to get λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m.

items.explain:
Rearrange: λ = v ÷ f
λ = 340 ÷ 680 = 0.50 m

Check: 680 × 0.50 = 340 m/s. It matches.

items.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic wave has a longer wavelength than visible light but a shorter wavelength than microwaves?
options: Infrared
Ultraviolet
Radio waves
X-rays
why: Ultraviolet is on the other side of visible light, so its wavelength is shorter than visible light's, not longer.
Radio waves have even longer wavelengths than microwaves, so they do not fit between microwaves and visible light.
X-rays have much shorter wavelengths than visible light. They are near the high-energy end of the spectrum.
items.explain: Longest to shortest wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. The only type between microwaves and visible light is infrared.

items.prompt: A series circuit contains a 10 Ω resistor and a 14 Ω resistor. A meter shows a current of 0.50 A. Using V = IR, what is the voltage of the battery, in volts?

mistakes.why: You used only the 10 Ω resistor. In series, add the resistances: 10 + 14 = 24 Ω, then V = 0.50 × 24 = 12 V.
You used only the 14 Ω resistor. Both are in the single loop: R<sub>total</sub> = 24 Ω, so V = 0.50 × 24 = 12 V.
48 is 24 ÷ 0.50. To find voltage, multiply current by resistance: 0.50 × 24 = 12 V.

items.explain:
Series: Rtotal = 10 + 14 = 24 Ω
V = I × R = 0.50 × 24 = 12 V

Using only one resistor gives 5 V or 7 V; both resistors share the same current in a series loop.

vocab.def: The ability to do work or cause change, measured in joules (J).
vocab.example: Gasoline stores energy that a car engine uses to move the car.

vocab.def: The energy an object has because it is moving. KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>.
vocab.example: A 2 kg ball rolling at 3 m/s has ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J of kinetic energy.

vocab.def: Stored energy an object has because of its height above the ground. PE = mgh.
vocab.example: A 10 kg box on a 2 m shelf has 10 × 9.8 × 2 = 196 J.

vocab.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it only changes form or moves between objects.
vocab.example: As a ball falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy.

vocab.def: The energy of moving particles in a substance; what we feel as heat.
vocab.example: Rubbing your hands together turns kinetic energy into thermal energy.

vocab.def: Heat transfer through direct contact between objects or particles.
vocab.example: A metal pan handle gets hot on the stove.

vocab.def: Heat transfer by the movement of a warm liquid or gas.
vocab.example: Hot air rising from a heater circulates through a room.

vocab.def: Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space.
The distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest, in meters. Symbol: λ.
vocab.example: Ocean waves with crests 10 m apart have a wavelength of 10 m.

vocab.def: The number of waves that pass a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
vocab.example: A tuning fork that vibrates 440 times per second has a frequency of 440 Hz.

vocab.def: The height of a wave from its resting position; larger amplitude means more energy.
vocab.example: A loud sound has a larger amplitude than a quiet one.

vocab.def: The full range of electromagnetic waves, from radio waves (longest wavelength) to gamma rays (shortest).
vocab.example: Microwaves, visible light, and X-rays are all parts of the spectrum.

vocab.def: The push that moves electric charges through a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The rate at which electric charge flows, measured in amperes (A).
vocab.example: A lamp might draw 0.5 A of current.

vocab.def: How strongly a material opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).
vocab.example: A 9 V battery across a 3 Ω resistor gives a current of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 A.

notes:
Study Notes: Energy and Waves

Formulas (units)

  • KE = ½mv2 — J; m in kg; v in m/s
  • PE = mgh — J; g = 9.8 m/s2; h in m
  • v = f × λ — m/s; f in Hz; λ in m
  • V = I × R — volts; amps (A); ohms (Ω)
    I = V ÷ R   R = V ÷ I
  • Series: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + …; one break, all off. Parallel: separate paths; others stay on.

Key Rules

  • Energy is never created or destroyed; it changes form.
  • “Lost” energy = thermal energy from friction.
  • Efficiency = useful out ÷ total in × 100%.
  • Falling: PE at top = KE at bottom (no friction).
  • Double speed → 4 × KE. Double height → 2 × PE.
  • Heat flows warm → cool, never the reverse on its own.
  • Same voltage, more resistance → less current.
  • Bigger amplitude → more energy (louder, brighter).
  • Same wave speed: double f → half λ.

Forms of Energy

Kinetic: motion, thermal, sound, electrical
Potential: gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear
Light: carried by electromagnetic waves

Electromagnetic Spectrum

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma
Longer λ, lower f, less energy  →  shorter λ, higher f, more energy

Waves

Mechanical (sound, water) need matter. Electromagnetic waves travel through space at 3.0 × 108 m/s.
